Getting Started with xpam

Source: vignettes/xpam-intro.Rmd
xpam-intro.Rmd

Overview

The xpam package builds geographic presence-absence matrices (PAMs) from species range polygons. A PAM is a sites-by-species binary table where rows are grid cells and columns are species; a cell contains 1 when the species range overlaps that cell and 0 otherwise.

PAMs are a fundamental data structure in macroecology and biogeography, used for computing species richness, range-diversity plots, co-occurrence analyses, and input to conservation-prioritisation algorithms.

Installation 

# From CRAN
install.packages("xpam")

# Development version (identical code to the public repository)
# install.packages("remotes")
# remotes::install_github("alrobles/xpam")

Quick Start

The core workflow has two steps:

  1. Load species range polygons as a terra::SpatVector.
  2. Call get_geo_pam() with a desired grid resolution.
library(xpam)

# Step 1: load example data (Rodentia of Mexico)
shp <- get_rodentia_mexico()
shp

# Step 2: build the PAM at 1-degree resolution
pam_result <- get_geo_pam(shp, res = 1)
head(pam_result)

The result is a tibble. The first two columns (x, y) are cell centroids; the remaining columns are species, coded as 1/0.

Adjusting Resolution

The res argument controls the grid cell size in the same units as the CRS (decimal degrees for EPSG:4326): Higher resolution → more grid cells → finer spatial detail.

# Fine resolution (0.5 degree ~ 55 km at the equator)
pam_fine <- get_geo_pam(shp, res = 0.5)
dim(pam_fine)

# Coarse resolution (2 degrees ~ 220 km)
pam_coarse <- get_geo_pam(shp, res = 2)
dim(pam_coarse)

Computing Species Richness

Once you have a PAM, species richness per cell is just a row sum:

pam_result$richness <- rowSums(pam_result[, -(1:2)])

# Quick map with base R
plot(pam_result$x, pam_result$y,
     cex  = sqrt(pam_result$richness) * 0.3,
     pch  = 15,
     col  = hcl.colors(max(pam_result$richness))[pam_result$richness],
     xlab = "Longitude",
     ylab = "Latitude",
     main = "Rodentia Species Richness — Mexico")

Environmental Space

The package also provides a WorldClim PCA raster for environmental analyses:

world_pca <- get_world_pca()
terra::plot(world_pca)

The streaming engine

get_geo_pam() builds the raster in memory, so it is meant for small inputs. For continent- or global-scale work the package provides a streaming native engine (C++17, OpenMP, GDAL): it rasterises geometries or bins occurrence records straight from disk and never materialises a dense matrix.

The engine is driven by three functions. They share the same occurrence source (occ, occ_file or occ_polygons) and the same raster inputs (env_files):

  • pam_env_engine() returns marginals only – richness per bin and footprint per species;
  • pam_incidence() returns the PAM itself as a sparse matrix;
  • pam_jaccard() computes species-by-species (or site-by-site) Jaccard similarity from the same incidence.
# Environmental PAM marginals straight from raster files
eng <- pam_env_engine(
  env_files    = c("bio01.tif", "bio12.tif"),
  occ_polygons = "ranges.gpkg",
  poly_field   = "sciname",
  nbs          = c(30, 30)
)
eng$richness   # species per environmental bin
eng$footprint  # bins occupied per species
# The PAM itself, as a sparse units x species matrix
inc <- pam_incidence(
  env_files    = c("bio01.tif", "bio12.tif"),
  occ_polygons = "ranges.gpkg",
  poly_field   = "sciname",
  space        = "env",
  format       = "dgCMatrix"
)
dim(inc$pam)
# Pairwise Jaccard between species, from the same incidence
jac <- pam_jaccard(
  env_files    = c("bio01.tif", "bio12.tif"),
  occ_polygons = "ranges.gpkg",
  poly_field   = "sciname",
  space        = "env"
)
dim(jac$jaccard)

For geographic space pass space = "geo": env_files then supplies only the grid geometry and the units are terra cell numbers.

# Geographic PAM: raster cells as units, ranges rasterised on the fly
geo <- pam_incidence(
  env_files    = "template.tif",
  occ_polygons = "ranges.gpkg",
  poly_field   = "sciname",
  space        = "geo"
)
geo$nnz

The engine is built for scale, so the resource limits are explicit rather than silent: max_bitset_mb caps the shared bitset, max_out_mb caps the size of an incidence that may be marshalled back into R, and threads controls OpenMP parallelism (OMP_THREAD_LIMIT is respected).

GDAL is optional. has_gdal() reports whether the installed build has it; when it does not, the engine functions stop with an informative error and the terra-based dense path keeps working.

Using Your Own Data

You can pass any terra::SpatVector that has a sciname column: each unique value of sciname becomes a column in the output PAM.

library(terra)

my_shapes <- vect("path/to/my_ranges.shp")
names(my_shapes)
# [1] "sciname" "family" "order"  ...

my_pam <- get_geo_pam(my_shapes, res = 0.25)
